segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: What was the word for nothing?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Nada.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Nada. And nobody?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Nadie?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Yes, nadie.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: What was the word for more, like in more late or later?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Más. Más tarde.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So if you add más to nada or nadie, you get else.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So más can also mean else, like nadie más. What does that mean, nadie más?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Nobody else.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Nobody else. ¿Nada más?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Nothing else.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Nothing else. Good.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So how would you say, I didn't eat anything else? I didn't eat anything else.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: No comí anything?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So we have the double negative, no? So we'll say, I didn't eat nothing else. Nothing more.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: No comí nada más.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. No comí nada más. I didn't eat anything else. Good.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Didn't you eat anything else? Speaking informally. Didn't you eat anything else?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: I forgot the informal for past.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: You have the S in there which relates to you informal, and you also have the T in there.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: No comiste.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Which also relates to you informal, that T, no? But in a different way, but they're both in there and they will help you remember that ending: comiste.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Didn't you eat anything else?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: No comiste nada más?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. ¿No comiste nada más? What was to see?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Ver.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Ver. I saw?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Verí? Yeah, sorry, vi.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Vi. Good! You got the ending right. He saw?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Vio.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Vio. Good. You saw, speaking informally?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Viste.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Viste. We saw?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Vimos.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Vimos. And they saw?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Vieron.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Vieron.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: The accent's on the E.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Yes, vieron. So that's our set: vi, vio, vimos, viste, vieron.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Didn't you see me last night? Speaking informally. Didn't you see me last night?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: No me viste anoche?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. ¿No me viste anoche? Time in the sense of occasion, no, like when we say once, we mean one time, or when we say again, we mean another time, is vez. Vez. V-E-Z.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So in Spain this will sound like vez, vez.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Vez.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: This is a feminine word. So how would you say one time, or once?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Una vez.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Una vez. So how would you say, I saw him once?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Lo vi una vez.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Lo vi una vez. Good. How would you say I saw them once?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Los vi una vez.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Los vi una vez. They saw them once?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Los vieron una vez.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Los vieron una vez. How do you think you would say one more time? One more time, how do you think you would say that?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Una vez más.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Yes, una vez más, good. So you could say something like, I want to see them one more time. I want to see them one more time. How would you say that?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Quiero verlos una vez más.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Quiero verlos una vez más. I want to see them one more time, once more. What was the word for we? The word for we?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Nosotros.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Nosotros, good. Now nosotros is actually the combination of nos, like how we have in us, and otros, which means others. So we is kind of like us others.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: How would you say another time? And you don't say an other time in Spanish, you just say other time, so you don't need an, huh? So, another time?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Otra vez.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Otra vez, good. We can take this otros, we can work backwards to get otra, otra vez.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So you can use this like again, no? Otra vez, another time. So you could say, I want to see them again. I want to see them again.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Quiero verlos otra vez.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Quiero verlos otra vez. What was to leave or to go out?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Salir.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Salir, good. And what was to dance, related to ballerina?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Bailar.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Bailar. So how would you ask informally, did you go out to dance again? Did you go out to dance again? Speaking informally.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Saliste a bailar otra vez?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Very good. Saliste a, because we have this verb of motion of coming and going, ¿saliste a bailar otra vez? Good. What was to speak?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Hablar.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Hablar. And I spoke?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Hablé.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Hablé. He spoke, she spoke, it spoke, you formal spoke?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Habló.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Habló. We spoke?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Hablamos.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Hablamos. You informal?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Hablaste.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Hablaste. And they?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Hablaron.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Hablaron, well done. To arrive, to arrive was llegar.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Llegar.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Llegar. How would you say you arrived informally?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Llegaste.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Llegaste. Did you arrive late again? Did you arrive late again?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: So llegaste tarde otra vez?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. ¿Llegaste tarde otra vez? Did you arrive late again? Good. What was my house?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Mi casa.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Mi casa. How would you say, he arrived late to my house again? So he arrived late to my house again.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Llegó tarde a mi casa otra vez.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Llegó tarde a mi casa otra vez. Or llegó a mi casa tarde otra vez. This is flexible.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: How would you say, he arrived at my house again wanting to speak with me? He arrived at my house, to my house, again wanting to speak with me.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Llegó a mi casa otra vez

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Very good. Wanting?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Is it querer to to want? Querer.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Yes.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: So queriendo, queriendo hablar conmigo.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Llegó a mi casa otra vez queriendo hablar conmigo.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So we saw that we don't use the -ing in Spanish nearly half as much as we do in English. In English we really overuse the -ing, but this is one situation where we do want it, in structures like this. He arrived at my house again wanting to speak with me: llegó a mi casa otra vez queriendo hablar conmigo. Good.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So my house is mi casa. Your house, speaking informally, is tu casa. Tu casa.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Tu casa.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: You might have heard the expression "mi casa es tu casa". What does that mean?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: My house is your house.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: If you want to say at what time, you say at what hour. How would that be?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: A qué hora.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Hora. Here we use hora: a qué hora. Good.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So how would you say, at what time did they arrive at your house, to your house? At what time did they arrive at your house?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: A qué hora llegaron a tu casa?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. ¿A qué hora llegaron a tu casa? Very good. At what time did they arrive at your house or to your house? Good.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: If you say a la vez, a la vez, it means at the same time. Like in English when we say at a time, a la vez, two at a time we can say in English, this is at the time, at the same time, a la vez.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So you might want to say, everybody arrived at my house at the same time. What was the word for all?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Todo.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Todo, good. If you make this plural, todos, you get everybody. Everybody. Or you might also hear in Spanish todo el mundo, all the world, to say everybody, but todos is very common.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So everybody arrived at my house at the same time.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Todos llegaron a mi casa a la vez.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Todos llegaron a mi casa a la vez. Todos llegaron a la vez a mi casa. Flexible.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: What was to find or to encounter?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Encontrar.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Encontrar. And I found?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Encontré.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Encontré. I didn't find anything else in your house. What was your house again?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Tu casa.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Tu casa, good. I didn't find anything else, nothing more, in your house. I didn't find anything else in your house.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: No encontré nada más en tu casa.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. I didn't find anything else in your house: no encontré nada más en tu casa. Good. So we have mi casa, tu casa.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Now the word for our is nuestro. Our house is nuestra casa. Nuestra casa. We can see the O splitting of nosotros there in nuestro, nuestra. So that's our.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So how would you say, did you visit our house? What is to visit? Visitation?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Visitación. Visitar.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. So did you visit our house? Speaking informally.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Visitaste nuestra casa?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. ¿Visitaste nuestra casa? Did you visit our house? How would you say we are with our friends? How do you think you would say that? We are with our friends.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: We are with, what to be do you think we will use?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Estar.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Estar, because we are with, no, location. Good. So we are with our friends.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Estamos con nuestros amigos.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good, nuestros amigos. Good, you make it plural to match amigos. We are with our friends. What if we meant all female friends?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Estamos con nuestras amigas.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Estamos con nuestras amigas. How would you say I am with my friends? I am with my friends.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Estoy con, is it mis amigos?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Yes. Estoy con mis amigos.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So the words for possession, mi, tu, nuestro, can change for number to match the number: mi amigo, mis amigos. And if it ends in O like nuestro, it can change for gender as well: nuestro amigo, nuestra amiga. So we have mi, my, tu, your, nuestro or nuestra, our.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: For his, her, their, your speaking formally, for all of that we have the same word, which is su. Su. S-U.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Su.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Su. So how would you say, I want to go to his house? I want to go to his house.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Quiero ir a su casa.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Quiero ir a su casa. I want to go to his house. How would you say I want to go to their house?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Quiero ir a su casa.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Quiero ir a su casa. So it's the same. If you put it in plural or not refers to the things that are possessed, not the possessors. So avoid any temptation to say sus because you mean they. You're only going to say sus if you're saying houses, for example.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So if you were to say I want to go to their houses, there you can put it in plural. How would that be?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Quiero ir a sus casas.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Quiero ir a sus casas. And I want to go to his houses? I want to go to his houses?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Quiero ir a sus casas.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Exactly, the same. Quiero ir a sus casas. So these possessive words, mi, tu, nuestro, su, they refer to the thing being possessed rather than the possessor when they're changing.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: If you want to say my own house, if you want to say my own house or my very own house, you can say mi propia casa, like property. Mi propia casa.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Mi propia casa.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. How would you say my own car?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Mi propio auto.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Mi propio auto. The word for eye in Spanish, not I as in you, I as in the the two things in your head, is ojo. Ojo. O-J-O, ojo.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Ojo.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Ojo. How would you say my own eyes? My own eyes.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Mi propios ojos.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: There's some kind of disagreement going on in there.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Mis... Mis propios ojos.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. So I saw it with my own eyes. I saw it with my own eyes.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Lo vi con mis propios ojos.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Lo vi con mis propios ojos. Very good. How would you say I want to live in my own house?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: I want to live in my own house.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Quiero vivir en mi propio casa... mi propia casa.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Quiero vivir en mi propia casa. Good, I want to live in my own house. Good.
